events.title: Epic of Gilgamesh Compiled
events.blurb: Mesopotamian scribes compiled the standard version of a long cuneiform poem about a semi-legendary king of a Sumerian city, his wild-man companion, and a flood survivor they visit in search of immortality. Earlier Sumerian poems about the hero had been circulating for centuries; a single scribe, working in Akkadian, produced the integrated twelve-tablet version that survives. It is the oldest recognized work of narrative literature.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1200 BCE — standard Babylonian version attributed to the scribe Sin-liqe-unninni. The poem's flood narrative preceded the one in Genesis by at least 500 years. Rediscovered in fragments in 19th-century excavations of Nineveh.

events.title: The Tale of Genji
events.blurb: A Japanese noblewoman serving at the imperial court of a Heian-era empress completed a 54-chapter prose narrative following the life, loves, and political career of a fictional son of an emperor. Full of psychological interiority, metaphorical poetry, and a sophisticated unreliable narrator, it is widely regarded as the world's first modern novel. It was written over more than a decade and circulated in manuscript among the court.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1010 CE — Murasaki Shikibu. The earliest surviving complete manuscript dates from the 13th century. It has been translated into English several times; Arthur Waley's 1925-33 version introduced it to the West, but recent translations are preferred for accuracy.

events.title: Frankenstein Published
events.blurb: An anonymously published novel telling, through nested letters and narratives, the story of a Swiss medical student who assembles and animates a humanoid creature from stolen body parts. The creature, rejected by its creator, turns on him. The author, a 20-year-old English woman, had dreamed the core story two years earlier during a rainy holiday on Lake Geneva, when her host proposed everyone write a ghost story.
events.revealBlurb: January 1, 1818 — Mary Shelley (née Godwin), daughter of Mary Wollstonecraft and William Godwin. The Lake Geneva party included Percy Bysshe Shelley, Lord Byron, and John Polidori (whose own contribution became "The Vampyre," the first English-language vampire novel).

events.title: Rabindranath Tagore Wins Nobel
events.blurb: A 52-year-old Bengali polymath — poet, novelist, philosopher, composer, painter — was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, becoming the first non-European and the first Asian to receive the honour. The Swedish Academy specifically cited his English translation of his own Bengali poetry collection "Gitanjali." The award brought him international fame; at home in colonial India it cemented him as a national cultural figure.
events.revealBlurb: November 13, 1913 — Rabindranath Tagore. He renounced his British knighthood in 1919 after the Jallianwala Bagh Massacre. He composed the national anthems of both India ("Jana Gana Mana") and Bangladesh ("Amar Shonar Bangla"), two of three anthems he wrote for different countries.

events.title: 1984 Published
events.blurb: A 46-year-old English novelist, suffering from advanced tuberculosis on a remote Scottish island, published a dystopian novel depicting a totalitarian state where history is continuously rewritten, all speech is monitored, and a figurehead leader is omnipresent. He had been working on it for four years; he typed much of it lying in bed. He died of the disease seven months later. The book gave English a vocabulary for surveillance authoritarianism that has never been matched.
events.revealBlurb: June 8, 1949 — George Orwell (Eric Blair). Written on the island of Jura. "Big Brother," "doublethink," "thought police," "Newspeak," and "Orwellian" all entered English usage. The title's year was chosen by reversing 1948, the year he completed the draft.

events.title: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
events.blurb: An English writer who had been educating herself in French enlightenment philosophy published a 300-page treatise arguing that women appeared inferior only because they received inferior education, and that a rational republic required the rational education of both sexes. It was attacked, praised, and influential on both sides of the Atlantic. She died five years later from complications after childbirth.
events.revealBlurb: January 1792 — Mary Wollstonecraft. The child she died giving birth to was Mary Shelley, author of Frankenstein. Her husband, William Godwin, published an honest memoir after her death that destroyed her reputation for a century.

events.title: Seneca Falls Convention
events.blurb: Three hundred people, a third of them men, gathered for two days at a Methodist chapel in upstate New York for the first women's rights convention held in the United States. Participants approved a "Declaration of Sentiments" modelled on the Declaration of Independence, demanding legal equality in marriage, property, education, employment, and the franchise. Only one resolution — women's suffrage — passed by a narrow vote.
events.revealBlurb: July 19-20, 1848 — Seneca Falls, NY. Lead organizers Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott. Only one signer, 19-year-old Charlotte Woodward, lived to vote in a federal election 72 years later. She was 91 and bed-ridden on Election Day 1920 and could not make it to the polls.

events.title: UK Women Get the Vote
events.blurb: A British parliament, persuaded partly by the contribution of women to the wartime labour force, enfranchised women householders and university graduates aged 30 and over — extending the franchise to about 8.5 million new voters. Complete parity with men would take another decade. One of its first fruits was the election, shortly after, of a woman to the Commons, who declined to take her seat.
events.revealBlurb: February 6, 1918 — Representation of the People Act. The non-taking-her-seat member was Constance Markievicz, elected for Sinn Féin in Dublin; she refused to swear allegiance to the Crown. Women 21-29 got the vote in 1928.

events.title: 19th Amendment Ratified
events.blurb: Seven decades after a convention in upstate New York had narrowly resolved that women ought to vote, a Tennessee state legislator cast the deciding vote for his state's ratification — after reading a telegram from his mother urging him to do so. Women across the United States gained the national vote in time for the November presidential election, in which 8 million new voters participated.
events.revealBlurb: August 18, 1920 — the deciding vote was cast by Harry T. Burn, age 24. His mother's letter read: "Hurrah, and vote for suffrage. Don't keep them in doubt." The amendment was certified on August 26, now Women's Equality Day.

events.title: Margaret Thatcher Becomes PM
events.blurb: The leader of the British Conservative Party, a grocer's daughter who had studied chemistry at Oxford and later trained as a barrister, was invited by the monarch to form a government after her party won a sweeping parliamentary majority. She became the United Kingdom's first woman prime minister and would hold the office for 11 years — the longest continuous premiership of the 20th century.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1979 — she took office quoting St. Francis of Assisi on the doorstep: "Where there is discord, may we bring harmony." The next decade would be anything but that. She was forced to resign by her own cabinet in November 1990.

events.title: Sulla's March on Rome
events.blurb: When the Senate transferred his military command to a political rival, consul Lucius Sulla marched six legions across the pomerium — the sacred city boundary no Roman general had ever crossed in arms — and took Rome by force. It was the first time in the Republic's history that a sitting consul used his own army to seize the capital; most of his officers refused the order and resigned rather than obey.
events.revealBlurb: 88 BCE, Rome. After taking the city Sulla had his enemies declared public enemies, then left for his original campaign in Greece as if nothing unusual had happened. His opponent Marius promptly retook Rome, declared Sulla a criminal, and died of old age seven days into his seventh consulship.

events.title: Caesar Crosses the Rubicon
events.blurb: A Roman general returning from nine years of conquest in Gaul, forbidden by law from bringing his army across the small river marking the boundary of Italy proper, led a single legion across anyway — knowing the act constituted treason against the Republic. He was reportedly quoting a Greek tragedian: "the die is cast." His subsequent march on Rome ignited a four-year civil war, at the end of which he emerged as a dictator-for-life and the Republic ended in everything but name.
events.revealBlurb: January 10, 49 BCE — Julius Caesar with Legion XIII. "Alea iacta est" — "the die is cast" — is attributed to him crossing. The Rubicon itself is a small, easily missable river in northern Italy; its modern identity is still debated by historians. The phrase "crossing the Rubicon" has since become an English idiom.

events.title: Year of the Four Emperors
events.blurb: In a single calendar year, the Roman principate cycled through four rulers — Galba, Otho, Vitellius, and Vespasian — as competing legions backed their own generals in an open civil war. Vespasian, commanding troops in Judaea, won by securing Egypt's grain supply first and strangling Rome's food imports until the Senate gave in.
events.revealBlurb: 69 CE. Otho lost one battle, decided he didn't want more Romans to die for him, and stabbed himself — widely praised as his most noble act. Vitellius, who followed, spent his months in power eating. He was eventually dragged through Rome, publicly mocked, killed, and thrown in the Tiber.

events.title: Aurelian Reunifies the Empire
events.blurb: After the empire had fractured into three competing states, Emperor Aurelian defeated the Palmyrene Empire in the east — capturing its queen Zenobia — and then the breakaway Gallic Empire in the west, bringing Britain, Gaul, Spain, Syria, and Egypt back under a single ruler within five years of taking power. He then began building a massive new defensive wall around Rome itself.
events.revealBlurb: 274 CE. Queen Zenobia of Palmyra had claimed descent from Cleopatra and ruled a sophisticated court of scholars and poets while commanding legions across the Near East. After capture she was eventually settled near Tivoli and, according to some sources, married a Roman senator.

events.title: Deposition of Romulus Augustulus
events.blurb: The Germanic warlord Odoacer deposed the sixteen-year-old emperor Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna — a boy whose mocking nickname meant "Little Augustus" — and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople, informing the eastern emperor that the west no longer needed a separate ruler. Odoacer spared Romulus's life, finding him too young and too minor to bother executing, and exiled him to a villa in Campania on a pension.
events.revealBlurb: September 4, 476 CE. The last western emperor's name combined the city's legendary founder and its first emperor — an irony Roman writers noticed immediately. Contemporaries did not regard this moment as "the fall of Rome"; that framing came centuries later. The eastern empire in Constantinople continued for another 977 years.

events.title: Survivor Premieres
events.blurb: A CBS reality competition series premiered, dropping 16 Americans on a Malaysian island and instructing them to "outwit, outplay, outlast" each other in a game of voted-off eliminations for a million-dollar prize. The finale two months later drew 51 million viewers. The show's format — strangers in deprived conditions voting each other out week by week — launched the modern reality-TV boom and made "tribal council" a household phrase.
events.revealBlurb: May 31, 2000 — host Jeff Probst, season 1 winner Richard Hatch. Hatch was later convicted of tax evasion for failing to declare the million-dollar prize. The show has run 45 seasons as of 2024 and is still in production, a foundational text of unscripted American television.

events.title: YouTube Launched
events.blurb: Three former PayPal employees, reportedly frustrated that they couldn't easily share a video of a dinner party or (by an alternate legend) a wardrobe malfunction from a recent sporting event, registered a domain name for a video-sharing site. The site's first uploaded video, "Me at the zoo," was an 18-second clip of one of the founders standing in front of elephants at the San Diego Zoo. Google bought them for $1.65 billion in stock twenty months later.
events.revealBlurb: February 14, 2005 — Chad Hurley, Steve Chen, Jawed Karim. The "Me at the zoo" video is still online, with over 350 million views. Users now upload over 500 hours of video every minute.

events.title: Heath Ledger Dies
events.blurb: A 28-year-old Australian actor was found dead in his lower Manhattan apartment by a masseuse who had come for an appointment. The cause was an accidental overdose of six prescription medications, including painkillers, anti-anxiety drugs, and sleep aids. He had recently finished filming an intense performance as the Joker in a Batman film released six months later; his family and colleagues have long disputed the "Joker-drove-him-mad" narrative that emerged. He won a posthumous Academy Award for the role.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 2008 — Heath Ledger in NYC. Daughter Matilda (with Michelle Williams) was 2. His 2008 film "The Dark Knight" was one of the first films to benefit from the surge in digital IMAX releases. His posthumous Oscar made him the second actor ever to win a competitive acting Oscar after death.

events.title: "The Dress" Goes Viral
events.blurb: A 21-year-old Scottish woman posted a photograph of a dress on her Tumblr account asking for help settling a family argument — was it black and blue, or white and gold? The photo went viral overnight. Approximately 40 percent of viewers saw it as white and gold; 50 percent as black and blue. Vision scientists spent months examining why. The actual dress, in real life, was black and blue. The phenomenon became a landmark case study in how individual visual perception varies based on assumptions about ambient lighting.
events.revealBlurb: February 26, 2015 — Cecilia Bleasdale's photograph, posted by Caitlin McNeill. Roman Originals, who made the dress, saw a 560 percent spike in sales. Neuroscientists published papers on it for years. It revived serious research into color constancy and top-down visual processing.

events.title: David Bowie Dies
events.blurb: A 69-year-old English singer and songwriter died of liver cancer at his New York apartment, two days after releasing what turned out to be his final studio album. The album's cover art, title ("Blackstar"), and lyrics — which in retrospect clearly addressed death — had been a farewell that almost nobody had caught in real time. His decades of genre-shifting personas, starting with the glam-rock Ziggy Stardust in 1972, had made him one of the most influential musicians of the late 20th century. His death prompted an international wave of mourning.
events.revealBlurb: January 10, 2016 — David Bowie (David Robert Jones). Diagnosed 18 months earlier; kept the illness private. His final public appearance was at the premiere of his off-Broadway musical "Lazarus" in December 2015. 2016 became known as a year of many significant music deaths.

events.title: Harvey Publishes De Motu Cordis
events.blurb: A 50-year-old English royal physician published a 72-page Latin treatise correctly describing, for the first time, the circulation of the blood — with the heart as a muscular pump, arteries carrying blood outward, veins returning it, and the two sides of the heart circulating distinct streams between the body and the lungs. He had been working on the theory for nearly two decades and had presented earlier versions in lectures. The medical establishment largely ignored the book for a generation.
events.revealBlurb: 1628 — William Harvey, "Exercitatio Anatomica de Motu Cordis et Sanguinis in Animalibus." Harvey's practice lost patients initially as word spread of his heresy. He lived long enough to see the theory accepted; he died in 1657 at 79, still personally treating King Charles II.

events.title: Germ Theory of Fermentation Established
events.blurb: A French chemist demonstrated through carefully controlled experiments that fermentation and putrefaction were caused by specific living microorganisms rather than by spontaneous chemical processes, and that sterilising a broth and sealing it from the air could prevent spoilage indefinitely. The experiments demolished the theory of spontaneous generation and formed the empirical backbone of germ theory.
events.revealBlurb: 1859–1861 — Louis Pasteur's famous swan-neck flask experiments showed that sterilized broth stayed clear indefinitely until the curved neck was broken, letting airborne microbes in. He reportedly presented one surviving flask to the Academy in 1878 saying it had shown no signs of life in fifteen years. Some of those original flasks are still intact at the Pasteur Institute.

events.title: Ross Identifies Malaria Vector
events.blurb: A 40-year-old British army medical officer working in colonial India dissected an Anopheles mosquito that had fed on a patient with malarial fever and observed the malaria parasite's oocysts developing in the mosquito's stomach wall. He had been pursuing the mosquito-borne hypothesis, championed by his mentor in London, for years. The discovery transformed tropical-disease prevention into an enterprise of draining swamps and destroying mosquito breeding sites.
events.revealBlurb: August 20, 1897 — Ronald Ross in Secunderabad, India. He called it his "mosquito day." Ross won the 1902 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. The mentor who had championed the mosquito hypothesis, Patrick Manson, was quietly robbed of credit at the time but is now recognized as a co-founder of tropical medicine.

events.title: Insulin Administered to a Patient
events.blurb: A 14-year-old diabetic patient near death at a Toronto hospital received an injection of pancreatic extract prepared by two medical researchers after earlier formulations had failed due to impurities. The boy recovered, and researchers moved ward to ward injecting the remaining diabetic patients — transforming a death sentence into a manageable condition within weeks.

events.title: Human Genome Draft Published
events.blurb: Two groups — the international Human Genome Project consortium and the private company Celera Genomics, which had entered the race late with a competing methodology — simultaneously published their draft sequences of the 3 billion base pairs of the human genome in the journals Nature and Science. The entries were the culmination of 11 years of work and a vast investment of computing and laboratory resources. Humans had roughly 21,000 genes — far fewer than most biologists had predicted.
events.revealBlurb: February 12, 2001 — publications in Nature (consortium) and Science (Celera). The "finished" version of the sequence arrived in 2003. Sequencing a human genome now costs about $200 (down from $2.7 billion) and takes a day.

events.title: Ptolemy's Almagest Completed
events.blurb: A Greco-Roman astronomer working in Alexandria compiled the most comprehensive mathematical model of the heavens yet assembled, describing the apparent motions of the Sun, Moon, planets, and 1,022 fixed stars using a system of circles and epicycles centred on the Earth. The work synthesised centuries of Babylonian and Greek observations and provided a predictive model accurate enough to calculate planetary positions centuries into the future.
events.revealBlurb: c. 150 CE — the Almagest was so complete that it suppressed further progress in astronomy for over a millennium. Astronomers kept patching it rather than questioning its Earth-centred premise. The name comes from the Arabic al-majisṭī, meaning "the greatest" — added by Islamic scholars who translated and preserved the text when European copies were lost.

events.title: Electron Announced
events.blurb: During a lecture at a London scientific institution, a physicist announced that cathode rays were composed of particles roughly one-thousandth the mass of a hydrogen atom — the first demonstration that atoms were not the smallest units of matter. The particles were initially called "corpuscles"; the modern name came from a suggestion by an Irish physicist the same year.
events.revealBlurb: April 30, 1897 — J.J. Thomson's discovery won him the Nobel Prize in 1906, and his son George Thomson won a separate Nobel in 1937 for proving the electron was a wave. Father and son together proved it was a particle and a wave — one of physics' neatest family rivalries.

events.title: Continental Drift Hypothesis Presented
events.blurb: A German meteorologist proposed that Earth's continents were once joined in a single supercontinent that had since broken apart and drifted slowly across the ocean floor, citing the geometric fit of coastlines, matching fossil records on opposite sides of the Atlantic, and ancient glacial scour marks in tropical regions. The geological community's response was immediate and largely hostile.
events.revealBlurb: January 6, 1912 — Alfred Wegener's hypothesis was mocked at a major American geological meeting in 1926, where a speaker suggested geologists should "be instantly prepared to disregard" it. Wegener died on a Greenland expedition in 1930. The mechanism he was missing — seafloor spreading — was found by Harry Hess in the 1960s.

events.title: Pluto Discovered
events.blurb: A young farm-hand-turned-astronomer at an Arizona observatory found a faint, slowly moving point of light by comparing photographic plates taken several days apart — a new body at the edge of the solar system. The discovery completed a decadelong search for a hypothetical ninth planet believed to be perturbing the orbits of the outermost known worlds.
events.revealBlurb: February 18, 1930 — Clyde Tombaugh was 24 and had never attended university. The name "Pluto" was suggested by Venetia Burney, an 11-year-old girl in Oxford, via her grandfather. In 2006, the International Astronomical Union reclassified Pluto as a "dwarf planet," prompting widespread public outrage and several state legislatures to pass resolutions disagreeing.

events.title: Plate Tectonics Theory Accepted
events.blurb: After decades of ridicule, a theory holding that Earth's crust is fractured into massive slabs drifting centimetres each year was vindicated by magnetic stripe patterns mapped on either side of mid-ocean ridges. The pattern matched predictions for seafloor spreading, explaining continental shapes, mountain ranges, and earthquake zones in a single framework.
events.revealBlurb: 1967–68 — the "plate tectonics revolution". Alfred Wegener had proposed continental drift in 1912 and been mocked for it; he died in 1930 on an expedition in Greenland. Geologists officially accepted his core idea thirty-seven years after his death.

events.title: Watt's Separate Condenser Patent
events.blurb: A Scottish instrument maker received a patent for a steam engine design that used a separate condenser chamber, dramatically reducing fuel consumption. Unlike earlier designs that wasted energy reheating the main cylinder on every stroke, the new engine converted roughly 75% more heat into mechanical work.

events.title: Watt's Separate Condenser
events.blurb: A 33-year-old Scottish instrument maker, repairing a model of a 50-year-old atmospheric engine for a university natural philosophy class, realized its efficiency was fatally compromised by repeatedly heating and cooling the same cylinder. His solution — a separate condensing vessel — cut fuel consumption by 75 percent. Patented four years later, the improved engine could be sited anywhere, not only beside a coal pit, and became the prime mover of 19th-century industry.
events.revealBlurb: 1765 insight; January 5, 1769 patent — James Watt. His decade-long partnership with Birmingham industrialist Matthew Boulton commercialized the engine. The unit of power is named for him. "Horsepower" was also his invention, a marketing metric.

events.title: Haymarket Bombing, Chicago
events.blurb: At a labor rally in Chicago's Haymarket Square called to protest the police killing of striking workers the previous day, an unknown person threw a dynamite bomb into a column of police officers, killing seven officers and at least four civilians in the ensuing explosion and gunfire. The incident became the defining trauma of American labor radicalism and led to the hanging of four men for conspiracy, despite the bomber's identity never being established.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1886 — Haymarket Square, Chicago. Nobody has ever been identified as the bomber. Governor John Altgeld pardoned the surviving defendants in 1893, calling the trial a miscarriage of justice — and was destroyed politically for it. The date May 4 became International Workers' Day in much of the world as a result of the Haymarket executions.

events.title: Coca-Cola Invented
events.blurb: An Atlanta pharmacist, a former Confederate officer who had become addicted to morphine following a Civil War injury, mixed a flavoured syrup of coca leaves and kola nuts with carbonated water at a downtown soda fountain and began selling it by the glass as a "brain tonic." The formula initially contained a small amount of cocaine; it was removed in 1903. The modestly popular local beverage grew into the world's most recognized consumer brand.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1886 — John Pemberton at Jacobs' Pharmacy, Atlanta. Pemberton sold the formula piecemeal in ill health; Asa Griggs Candler consolidated ownership and built the business. Coca-Cola's secret recipe, "Merchandise 7X," is supposedly known to only two executives at any time.

events.title: Wright Brothers' First Flight
events.blurb: Two American bicycle-shop owners from Dayton, Ohio achieved the first sustained, controlled, powered flight of a heavier-than-air aircraft on a windswept dune at the Outer Banks of North Carolina. The first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 36 metres — about the wingspan of a modern commercial airliner. They made three more flights that morning; the fourth covered 260 metres in 59 seconds. Few newspapers reported the achievement; commercial aviation took another three decades to arrive.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1903 — Orville and Wilbur Wright at Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, NC. The flyer is now in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum. The pair spent 4 years after their first flight battling patent disputes and litigation rather than manufacturing planes.

events.title: ENIAC Unveiled
events.blurb: Engineers at an American university publicly demonstrated an 27-tonne general-purpose electronic computer, filling a 30 by 15 metre room with 17,468 vacuum tubes, 10,000 capacitors, and 6,000 switches. The machine calculated artillery-shell trajectories 2,400 times faster than a human with an adding machine. Programming it required physically rewiring hundreds of cables; the programmers — all women — had to crawl inside to swap plugs.
events.revealBlurb: February 15, 1946 — University of Pennsylvania. Designers J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly. Programmers: Kay McNulty, Betty Jennings, Betty Snyder, Marlyn Wescoff, Fran Bilas, and Ruth Lichterman. They were not invited to the unveiling dinner; their faces were cropped out of celebratory photos for decades.

events.title: Transistor Invented
events.blurb: Three physicists at an American industrial research laboratory demonstrated a working point-contact transistor — a tiny semiconductor device made from germanium that could amplify electrical signals without the vacuum tubes, heat, and bulk then required. Within a decade the invention had reshaped electronics; within five decades, billions of its descendants would fit on a single silicon chip smaller than a fingernail.
events.revealBlurb: December 23, 1947 — John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley at Bell Labs. They shared the 1956 Nobel. Shockley's later semiconductor company, though commercially a failure, seeded Silicon Valley through the departure of its "Traitorous Eight" founders of Fairchild Semiconductor.

events.title: Altair 8800 Released
events.blurb: A cover article in an American hobbyist electronics magazine featured a $397 kit-build computer based on the Intel 8080 microprocessor, aimed at hardware enthusiasts willing to solder circuit boards and toggle binary instructions with front-panel switches. The magazine received over 2,000 kit orders in the first month. Among the Harvard students who saw the cover and wrote a BASIC interpreter for the machine were Bill Gates and Paul Allen.
events.revealBlurb: January 1975 — MITS Altair 8800, on the cover of Popular Electronics. Gates and Allen's BASIC would become the founding product of Microsoft. The Altair is universally credited as the first commercially successful microcomputer.

events.title: iPhone Announced
events.blurb: A California computer company's co-founder unveiled a new class of mobile phone at a San Francisco conference, combining a widescreen iPod, a mobile internet browser, and a phone into a single slim device controlled entirely by a multi-touch finger-driven screen. He dialled a coffee shop on stage to demonstrate. Nokia's executives watching the announcement reportedly laughed at its lack of a physical keyboard; BlackBerry's CEO later admitted they also underestimated it.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 2007 — Steve Jobs at Macworld. It went on sale June 29. The original did not support 3G, had no copy-and-paste, and shipped without an App Store — those all came in subsequent years. Apple now makes over $200 billion a year just from iPhones.

events.title: iPad Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company released a 9.7-inch tablet — something between a smartphone and a laptop — running the same operating system as its phone. The product's name had been mocked in advance for rhyming with certain feminine-hygiene products; the device itself went on to redefine a computing form factor that previous attempts by Microsoft and others had never managed to make stick. It sold 3 million units in its first 80 days.
events.revealBlurb: April 3, 2010 — Apple iPad. Steve Jobs' last major product launch. "I think we have a winner here," he said at the introduction. Microsoft's Bill Gates had been pushing tablet PCs for a decade; Apple's combination of software, battery, and price finally made the form factor work.

events.title: Prabhat Film Company Founded
events.blurb: Five filmmakers and one jeweller-financier pooled ₹15,000 in a Kolhapur courtyard and established a studio whose name meant "Dawn" — it would go on to produce landmark Marathi and Hindi films through the 1930s, win the first Venice Film Festival prize awarded to an Asian film, and whose abandoned compound would later house the country's national film school.
events.revealBlurb: June 1, 1929 — founded by V. Shantaram and associates. Their 1936 film Sant Tukaram won a Venice award. When the studio folded in 1953, its Pune premises became the site of the Film and Television Institute of India.

events.title: Kalidas Released — First Tamil Talkie
events.blurb: A mythological musical about the Sanskrit poet Kalidasa opened at Kinema Central in Madras on Diwali and became simultaneously the first sound film in Tamil and the first in Telugu — the hero singing in Telugu, the heroine speaking Tamil, a third actor delivering dialogue in Hindi, making it a multilingual sound experiment disguised as a devotional drama.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1931 — directed by H.M. Reddy, just months after Alam Ara introduced sound to India. A young actor billed only as L.V. Prasad played a cameo; he would later become one of South India's most powerful film producers. The film is now preserved at the National Film Archive.

events.title: Kismet Released
events.blurb: A Bombay Talkies crime film with an unambiguous anti-hero — the lead character is a thief and a cad — opened in the depths of winter during a bitter internal dispute that was tearing the studio apart, yet became the first film in Indian cinema history to gross ₹1 crore. At a Calcutta cinema it ran for 187 consecutive weeks, a record that stood for 32 years.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 1943, Bombay. Directed by Gyan Mukherjee, starring Ashok Kumar. Its patriotic song "Door Hato Ae Duniyawalon" — aimed at colonial occupation without naming it — spread through cities as independence agitation intensified. The British censors initially approved it without grasping the subtext.

events.title: Pyaasa Released
events.blurb: A poet who the city believes to be dead wanders through venal publishers and indifferent relatives in a film Guru Dutt both directed and starred in, constructing one of Indian cinema's most sustained indictments of commercialised culture through Sahir Ludhianvi's Urdu verse set to S.D. Burman's music. Time magazine later placed it among the 100 greatest films ever made.
events.revealBlurb: February 22, 1957 — Guru Dutt's masterwork. The film was semi-autobiographical; Dutt was increasingly alienated from the Bombay film industry's values, an estrangement he did not survive — he died in 1964, aged 39. The song "Jaane Woh Kaise Log The" remains among the most covered in Hindi film music.

events.title: Sholay Released
events.blurb: A three-hour curry Western about two small-time criminals hired by a retired policeman to hunt a ruthless dacoit opened on India's Independence Day to a tepid first week before word-of-mouth turned it into the longest-running Indian film of all time. It played uninterrupted at a single Bombay theatre for five and a half years — 286 consecutive weeks.
events.revealBlurb: August 15, 1975. Director Ramesh Sippy. Amjad Khan as Gabbar Singh was nearly replaced because the scriptwriter thought his voice was too thin. The original ending showed Thakur killing Gabbar with spiked shoes — the censor board forced a reshoot. "Kitne aadmi the?" became a national catchphrase.

events.title: Alien and Sedition Acts Signed
events.blurb: President John Adams signed four statutes that extended the residency requirement for citizenship from five to fourteen years, empowered the president to expel foreigners deemed dangerous, and made it a crime to publish "false, scandalous, and malicious" criticism of the government. The laws were aimed largely at French immigrants and Republican newspaper editors who opposed the Federalist administration.
events.revealBlurb: July 14, 1798 — Philadelphia (the Sedition Act, last of the four). Twenty-five people were arrested and ten convicted under the Sedition Act — all of them Jefferson's supporters. Jefferson himself quietly wrote the Kentucky Resolutions arguing states could nullify federal law.

events.title: Battle of New Orleans
events.blurb: General Andrew Jackson's patchwork army of Tennessee frontiersmen, Louisiana militia, free Black soldiers, Choctaw warriors, and pirates under Jean Lafitte decisively routed an 8,000-strong British force attempting to seize New Orleans, killing or wounding roughly 2,000 redcoats while suffering fewer than 70 American casualties. The lopsided victory made Jackson a national hero and propelled him to the presidency.
events.revealBlurb: January 8, 1815 — Chalmette, Louisiana. The Treaty of Ghent ending the War of 1812 had been signed 15 days earlier — news hadn't arrived. The battle had zero effect on the war's official outcome but enormous effect on American mythology and Jackson's political career.

events.title: 18th Amendment: Prohibition Ratified
events.blurb: Nebraska became the 36th state to ratify the 18th Amendment, providing the three-fourths supermajority needed to ban the manufacture, sale, and transportation of intoxicating liquors in the United States. The amendment went into effect one year later, launching a 13-year experiment in moral legislation that spawned organized crime, enriched bootleggers, and ended with the 21st Amendment's repeal.
events.revealBlurb: January 16, 1919 — ratified in less than 11 months, the fastest major amendment in history to that point. Al Capone made an estimated $60 million a year ($1.1 billion today) during Prohibition.

events.title: Teapot Dome: Senate Investigation Opens
events.blurb: The Senate launched its first formal investigation into the Teapot Dome oil fields that autumn, following revelations that Interior Secretary Albert Fall had secretly leased federal naval petroleum reserves in Wyoming and California to private oil companies in exchange for personal cash loans and gifts totaling roughly $400,000. Fall would become the first U.S. Cabinet member ever convicted of a crime committed while in office.
events.revealBlurb: October 1923 — Washington, D.C. The oil companies that paid the bribes — Sinclair Oil and Pan American Petroleum — were acquitted at trial; only the man who took the bribes was convicted. President Harding died of a heart attack in August 1923, before the scandal fully broke.

events.title: Apollo 11: First Humans on the Moon
events.blurb: At 10:56 pm EDT that evening, astronaut Neil Armstrong stepped off the lunar module Eagle onto the surface of the Moon and became the first human being to walk on another world, watched live by an estimated 600 million people — roughly one-fifth of humanity. Buzz Aldrin joined him 19 minutes later; the two planted an American flag, collected samples, and departed after 2 hours and 31 minutes on the surface.
events.revealBlurb: July 20, 1969 — Sea of Tranquility, the Moon. Armstrong's famous line was supposed to be "one small step for a man" — he swears he said it; the transmission dropped the "a." Michael Collins orbited alone overhead for 21 hours while his crewmates were on the surface. President Nixon had a speechwriter prepare a statement in case they didn't make it back.

events.title: Cyrus the Great Takes Babylon
events.blurb: A Persian king who had already conquered Media, Lydia, and the Ionian cities entered the ancient city of Babylon without a fight, claiming to have been welcomed by its priests as the rightful king of the gods. His subsequent proclamation — known from a surviving cuneiform cylinder — repatriated exiled populations, restored local temples, and is sometimes described as the oldest surviving charter of human rights. The Persian Achaemenid Empire he founded became the largest the world had yet seen.
events.revealBlurb: October 29, 539 BCE — Cyrus II. The Cyrus Cylinder is now in the British Museum. The Hebrew Bible credits Cyrus with allowing the Judean exiles to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the Temple; he is the only non-Jewish figure called "messiah" in the Hebrew scriptures.

events.title: Alexander the Great Dies
events.blurb: A 32-year-old conqueror, having created an empire stretching from Macedonia to northwestern India in ten years of campaigning, died of fever (or poisoning — sources disagree) in a palace in a Mesopotamian capital while planning the next campaign, this one against Arabia. He left no clear heir; his generals divided the empire into warring successor states — the Hellenistic kingdoms — that shaped Mediterranean culture for the next three centuries.
events.revealBlurb: June 10 or 11, 323 BCE — Alexander III in Babylon. Asked on his deathbed to whom his empire should go, he reportedly said: "To the strongest." Competing theories for his death: malaria, typhoid, alcoholism, West Nile virus, poisoning by his general Antipater. His body was hijacked en route home by Ptolemy to Alexandria.

events.title: First Punic War Begins
events.blurb: The Roman Republic and the Carthaginian Empire, the two rising powers of the western Mediterranean, went to war over control of a large island between them. The conflict would last 23 years and transform Rome from a purely land-based power into a naval one — the Romans, ignorant of shipbuilding, reportedly reverse-engineered a captured Carthaginian warship to build their first fleet. Rome eventually won and imposed a crushing indemnity; the seed of two more wars was planted.
events.revealBlurb: 264 BCE — Rome vs. Carthage over Sicily. "Punic" comes from the Latin for "Phoenician," Carthage's origin. The Romans invented boarding bridges ("corvi") that turned sea battles into quasi-land battles they could win. Rome lost 700 ships over the course of the war, mostly to storms.

events.title: Augustus Becomes Emperor
events.blurb: The Roman Senate formally voted a new series of titles and powers to the victor of the civil wars that had ended the Republic — including "Augustus" (the revered), "Princeps" (first citizen), and various senatorial and tribunicial powers. The Republic's forms were maintained — the Senate met, consuls were elected — but real power now flowed through the man at the top. The Roman Empire had begun. Its first emperor would reign 41 years and die of natural causes in his 75th year.
events.revealBlurb: January 16, 27 BCE — Octavian accepts the title "Augustus." He preferred the title "Princeps"; only later emperors would unambiguously style themselves "Imperator." The month August is named for him. He outlived his designated heirs repeatedly; his step-son Tiberius eventually succeeded him in 14 CE.

events.title: The Antonine Plague
events.blurb: Soldiers returning from campaigns in Parthia brought a disease — almost certainly smallpox — that spread from the eastern frontier through every province of the empire over fifteen years. The physician Galen, the most famous doctor of his age, documented symptoms in detail from Rome itself; at the plague's peak witnesses recorded 2,000 deaths per day in the capital alone.
events.revealBlurb: 165–180 CE. Galen's treatment recommendation included keeping patients warm and feeding them milk — the best care available, and completely ineffective. The plague killed co-emperor Lucius Verus in 169 CE and may have killed up to 10% of the empire's total population.

events.title: First Public Film Screening
events.blurb: Two French brothers, sons of a portrait photographer, held the first commercial screening of projected motion pictures in the basement of a Paris café. The audience of 33 paid one franc each to watch ten short films — workers leaving a factory, a baby being fed, a boat leaving a harbor. Their cinematograph was both camera and projector; the film was 35mm. Within a year their operators were touring every continent.
events.revealBlurb: December 28, 1895 — Louis and Auguste Lumière at the Salon Indien du Grand Café, Paris. The apocryphal story that audiences ran screaming from the train-arriving film comes from a later screening. The Lumières thought cinema was "an invention without a future" and quickly moved on to other projects.

events.title: Metropolis Released
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Austrian director released a 153-minute silent epic — at the time the most expensive film ever made — set in a stratified future city where wealthy elites enjoy skyscraper gardens above an underground inferno of machine-tending workers. The film's visual language — robot maidens, neon skylines, expressionist sets — shaped science-fiction imagery for the next century. The premiere had uneven reception; 40 minutes of footage were later cut.
events.revealBlurb: January 10, 1927 — Fritz Lang at the UFA-Palast am Zoo, Berlin. A reasonably complete version was pieced together only in 2008, when a 16mm print from the 1930s was found in a Buenos Aires archive. The robot Maria was voted the most important film robot in history.

events.title: First Academy Awards
events.blurb: A 15-minute banquet at a Hollywood hotel awarded twelve statuettes — a 34 cm tall gilded figure of a knight standing on a reel of film — to films, actors, directors, and technicians selected by the newly formed Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. 270 people attended. The winners had been announced three months earlier. The whole ceremony received brief mention in the next day's Los Angeles Times, on page 10.
events.revealBlurb: May 16, 1929 — Hollywood Roosevelt Hotel. First Best Picture: "Wings." Best Actor: Emil Jannings. The bronze statuette's nickname, "Oscar," was supposedly coined by an Academy librarian who thought it resembled her Uncle Oscar; the story is almost certainly retrofitted.

events.title: Citizen Kane Released
events.blurb: A 25-year-old radio and theatre prodigy made his feature film directing debut with a quasi-biographical study of a newspaper tycoon, structurally organized as a series of flashback interviews about the man's last word ("Rosebud"). The film used deep-focus cinematography, low-angle setups, overlapping dialogue, and non-linear structure in ways that rewrote the cinematic grammar of the next 70 years. Its real-life subject, a media baron, tried to have every print destroyed.
events.revealBlurb: May 1, 1941 — Orson Welles, age 25. The target was William Randolph Hearst, who banned mention of the film in his newspapers. It lost Best Picture to "How Green Was My Valley." It tops nearly every "greatest films of all time" list.

events.title: Star Wars Released
events.blurb: A 33-year-old American director released a science-fiction film mashing up elements of samurai cinema, WWII dogfight pictures, and Joseph Campbell's monomyth theory, with groundbreaking effects assembled in a repurposed warehouse with a workforce assembled from scratch. The studio had cut his budget and expected the film to flop; one executive had retitled it "The Adventures of Luke Starkiller." Lines began forming at theatres on opening morning and did not stop for years.
events.revealBlurb: May 25, 1977 — George Lucas. He traded his directing salary for merchandising rights; he became a billionaire. The effects company he had to build from scratch, Industrial Light & Magic, became the industry standard for decades. Campbell wept watching the film.

events.title: Gutenberg Bible Printed
events.blurb: A goldsmith in a Rhine-valley city completed the first book printed in Europe using movable metal type — a Latin Bible set in 42 lines per page, bound in 180 copies. His press combined existing technologies — oil-based ink, a wine-press frame, cast-metal punches — into an invention that would be blamed for everything from the Reformation to the Renaissance to modern literacy.
events.revealBlurb: 1455 — Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz. Forty-nine copies are known to survive; roughly twenty are complete. Gutenberg himself was sued by his financier the same year and lost the press.

events.title: First Circumnavigation Complete
events.blurb: The last seaworthy ship of a Spanish expedition that had set out three years earlier with five vessels dropped anchor in the Guadalquivir River in Spain — the first ship ever to return to its port of departure after sailing completely around the world. Of the 270 men who had departed, 18 returned alive. Its captain, though no longer the expedition's original commander — who had been killed in the Philippines — had personally sailed the ship the entire way home.
events.revealBlurb: September 6, 1522 — Juan Sebastián Elcano aboard the Victoria. The voyage proved the earth was circumnavigable, and also forced the first adjustment of the ship's log by a day (a precursor to the concept of the International Date Line). Elcano himself died at sea in 1526, three ships into another expedition.

events.title: Pizarro Captures Atahualpa
events.blurb: A 54-year-old illiterate Spanish conquistador with 168 men and 62 horses ambushed, slaughtered the retinue of, and captured the ruler of the Inca Empire at an Andean town where the ruler had come to meet them for what he thought would be negotiations. The emperor offered to fill a room with gold to his height and two rooms with silver as ransom. The Spanish accepted, collected the ransom, and executed him anyway.
events.revealBlurb: November 16, 1532 — Francisco Pizarro vs. Atahualpa at Cajamarca. Atahualpa was garrotted on July 26, 1533. The Inca Empire's collapse was accelerated by smallpox, civil war, and Pizarro's exploitation of factionalism. Pizarro himself was murdered by rivals in 1541.

events.title: Copernicus's De Revolutionibus
events.blurb: A 70-year-old Polish mathematician and canon of a cathedral in Warmia died on the same day he was reportedly handed a freshly printed copy of the book he had been writing, revising, and withholding from publication for three decades. The book, On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, argued that the earth was a planet orbiting the sun, and that the apparent daily motion of the heavens was actually the earth's own rotation. It was placed on the Papal Index 73 years later.
events.revealBlurb: May 24, 1543 — Nicolaus Copernicus died. The book's printer, Andreas Osiander, had added an anonymous preface describing its heliocentrism as a mere mathematical convenience; Copernicus probably never saw that preface. Galileo, who openly defended heliocentrism, was tried for heresy in 1633.

events.title: Galileo's Telescope Observations
events.blurb: A 46-year-old Paduan university mathematics professor, having improved the magnification of a newly invented Dutch optical toy from 3x to 30x, pointed his telescope at the night sky. Over the following months he observed craters on the moon, four previously unknown moons circling Jupiter, phases of Venus, and individual stars resolvable in the milky white band of the Milky Way. His findings, published in a short Latin book, transformed astronomy.
events.revealBlurb: January 7, 1610 — Galileo Galilei observed Jupiter's moons from Padua. His book "Sidereus Nuncius" (The Starry Messenger) was rushed into print in March. The phases of Venus, observed later that year, were decisive evidence against the Ptolemaic earth-centered model.

events.title: Chandragupta Maurya Founds the Mauryan Empire
events.blurb: A young commander, advised by the strategist Chanakya, overthrew the last Nanda king of Magadha and seized the throne of Pataliputra. He then turned west to fill the power vacuum left by a retreating Macedonian army, consolidating the first empire to rule most of the Indian subcontinent under a single administration — complete with a spy network, standardized taxation, and a standing army of 600,000.
events.revealBlurb: c. 322 BCE — Chandragupta Maurya, guided by Chanakya, whose political treatise the Arthashastra is basically ancient India's "The Prince" — except sharper, and with chapters on crocodile moats.

events.title: Timur's Army Sacks Delhi
events.blurb: A Central Asian conqueror descended from the same steppes as Genghis Khan led 90,000 cavalry across the Indus, defeated the Tughluq sultan's army in a single battle, and spent weeks pillaging Delhi. Over 100,000 people were killed in the first days; the city smelled of corpses for months afterward. The artisans Timur took back to Samarkand included the craftsmen who would build the great monuments of his capital.
events.revealBlurb: December 1398 CE — Timur (Tamerlane), Delhi Sultanate. He departed having captured so many skilled craftsmen that Delhi was depopulated. Coin minting stopped, trade collapsed, and famine followed. The Sultanate technically survived but never recovered its former power — opening the door for Babur 128 years later.

events.title: The Taj Mahal Complex is Completed
events.blurb: Twenty-one years after construction began, the final elements of a riverside mausoleum complex — the mosque, the guesthouse, the great gateway, and the formal garden — were finished at Agra. The main dome of the central tomb had been completed five years earlier in 1648. The complex employed 20,000 workers and used marble inlaid with 28 varieties of semi-precious stones sourced from as far as Sri Lanka and Afghanistan.
events.revealBlurb: 1653 CE — Agra, Mughal Empire. Shah Jahan, who built it, was imprisoned in the Agra Fort across the river by his son Aurangzeb five years later. He reportedly spent his remaining years staring at the Taj from his marble window. The reflection pool was designed so he could see it even lying down.

events.title: Aurangzeb Imprisons His Father Shah Jahan
events.blurb: A Mughal emperor fell ill, setting off a fratricidal war among his four sons. The third son, Aurangzeb, outmaneuvered his brothers militarily and politically — defeating one at the Battle of Samugarh, executing another, driving the third into exile — then declared his father too weak to rule and locked him in the Agra Fort. Shah Jahan remained imprisoned there for eight years until his death, attended only by his devoted daughter Jahanara.
events.revealBlurb: July 1658 CE — Aurangzeb seizes the Mughal throne. Shah Jahan's prison quarters in Agra Fort had a view of the Taj Mahal across the river, built for his late wife. Contemporary sources say Jahanara placed a mirror so he could see it from his sickbed.

events.title: The Marathas Are Defeated at the Third Battle of Panipat
events.blurb: A Maratha army of 45,000 soldiers and 200,000 camp followers — including families who had brought their children on what they expected to be a triumphant northern campaign — faced an Afghan force under the Durrani king. After an eight-month standoff that left the Marathas starving, they were crushed in a single morning. Between 60,000 and 70,000 troops died in the battle; up to 40,000 prisoners were massacred the following day.
events.revealBlurb: January 14, 1761 — Ahmad Shah Durrani vs. Sadashivrao Bhau, Panipat. Fought on the same plain as two earlier world-changing battles. The Maratha defeat ended Hindu imperial ambitions and opened India to British expansion. It is said that barely a family in the Deccan was not in mourning afterward.

events.title: Amazon Founded
events.blurb: A former hedge-fund vice-president who had driven across the country from New York to Seattle with his wife, writing a business plan on the way, incorporated an online book retailer in the garage of a rented house in a Seattle suburb. He had chosen books because no single physical store could stock every book in print, but one big warehouse could. The company's first website was clunky; the logic was unstoppable.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1994 — Jeff Bezos. The company was originally called Cadabra; Bezos changed it after a lawyer misheard it as "cadaver." He considered and rejected relentless.com (now redirecting to Amazon).

events.title: Netscape IPO
events.blurb: A 16-month-old Silicon Valley company that had distributed free web browsers and had never turned a profit went public at $28 a share, opened at $71, and closed its first trading day at $58.25. Its 24-year-old co-founder was suddenly worth $58 million on paper. Wall Street had discovered the internet, and the next five years of stock-market mania had a starting gun.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 1995 — Netscape Communications. Co-founder Marc Andreessen ended up on the cover of Time two years later with the caption "The Kid Who Tamed the Web." Microsoft's bundled Internet Explorer would eventually kill Netscape; the company sold to AOL in 1999.

events.title: Wikipedia Launched
events.blurb: A 34-year-old internet entrepreneur who had been trying to build an online encyclopedia by paying credentialed experts to write and peer-review articles gave up on the slow model and switched to a radical alternative: a wiki, editable by anyone. The new version grew faster than expected. It had more articles in its first year than the slow-model version had produced in a previous eighteen months.
events.revealBlurb: January 15, 2001 — Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger. By 2007 Wikipedia had surpassed Britannica in size and approximately in accuracy. Today's English Wikipedia has over 6.9 million articles, and the full project runs in 340+ languages.

events.title: Netflix Launches Streaming
events.blurb: A decade-old Silicon Valley mail-order DVD rental company launched an online video-streaming service, initially offering subscribers limited hours of instant streaming on top of their physical DVD subscriptions. The library at launch had about 1,000 titles and required Internet Explorer. The service would eventually make the DVD operation so irrelevant that the company's own name became an anachronism (net-flicks via mail).
events.revealBlurb: January 16, 2007 — initial subscribers got 1 hour of streaming per dollar paid per month. In 2011, CEO Reed Hastings attempted to split DVDs into a sister brand "Qwikster"; the backlash was so severe he reversed within three weeks.

events.title: WikiLeaks Cablegate
events.blurb: A whistleblower-platform website and a consortium of five newspapers began publishing, in coordinated waves, 251,287 U.S. diplomatic cables leaked by a 22-year-old U.S. Army intelligence analyst. The cables ranged from the mundane to the explosive — unflattering private assessments of world leaders, evidence of corruption in allied governments, and revelations about civilian deaths in Iraq and Afghanistan. The leaker would face the longest sentence ever imposed for leaking U.S. government information.
events.revealBlurb: November 28, 2010 — leaker Chelsea Manning (then Bradley), sentenced to 35 years in 2013. Obama commuted her sentence in 2017. WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange lived in the Ecuadorian embassy in London from 2012 until 2019; he was released from UK custody in a 2024 plea deal.

events.title: Gallic Sack of Rome
events.blurb: Senone Gauls under their chieftain Brennus routed a Roman army at the Allia River, then entered a largely deserted Rome three days later and burned it for seven months. The sole holdout was the Capitoline Hill, where a sacred flock of geese allegedly woke the defenders when a Gallic night-assault crept up the cliffs.
events.revealBlurb: July 390 BCE, traditional (Polybius says 387). The ransom Brennus demanded in gold was agreed, but the Romans protested he was using rigged weights. Brennus reportedly threw his sword onto the scales and bellowed "Vae victis" — "Woe to the vanquished."

events.title: Octavian Becomes Augustus
events.blurb: The Roman Senate voted Gaius Octavian a new and previously unused title — Augustus, "the revered" — along with broad military command, tribunician power for life, and control of the key frontier provinces. He kept the word "republic" in circulation and called himself only "first citizen," but every structural mechanism of one-man rule was now legally his.
events.revealBlurb: January 16, 27 BCE. Augustus lived another 41 years and died of natural causes at 75 — an almost freakish accomplishment for a Roman emperor. His last words, spoken to friends, were reportedly: "Did I play the part well? Then applaud as I exit."

events.title: Great Fire of Rome
events.blurb: A fire that broke out near the Circus Maximus burned for nine days and destroyed or severely damaged ten of Rome's fourteen districts, leaving the majority of the population homeless. Emperor Nero, who was at Antium when the fire started, blamed the city's small Christian community and launched the first state-sanctioned persecution of Christians in Roman history.
events.revealBlurb: July 18, 64 CE. The story that Nero fiddled while Rome burned is almost certainly false — the fiddle didn't exist yet, and multiple sources place him outside the city at the time. Tacitus, writing fifty years later, noted that many Romans suspected Nero ordered the fire himself but that the charge was never proven.

events.title: Caracalla's Citizenship Edict
events.blurb: Emperor Caracalla issued a decree granting full Roman citizenship to every free person throughout the empire, erasing a 700-year distinction between citizen and non-citizen that had shaped Roman law, military service, and taxation. Modern historians debate whether the primary motive was ideological universalism or a straightforward need to expand the tax base.
events.revealBlurb: July 11, 212 CE. Caracalla's full name — Marcus Aurelius Severus Antoninus — was a collection of borrowed dynastic brands. "Caracalla" was the nickname Romans gave him, after a Gallic hooded cloak he popularised. He had his brother and co-emperor Geta killed months before signing this edict.

events.title: Permanent Division of the Roman Empire
events.blurb: On his deathbed in Mediolanum, Emperor Theodosius divided the empire between his two sons: eighteen-year-old Arcadius took the east with Constantinople, and ten-year-old Honorius took the west with its capital at Ravenna. No mechanism existed to reunite the two halves, and none ever did.
events.revealBlurb: January 17, 395 CE. Theodosius was the last man to rule the entire Roman Empire. His ten-year-old western heir Honorius grew up to be a notably passive emperor; later historians note that when told "Rome has fallen," he reportedly burst into tears — then relaxed when he learned it was the city, not his favourite hen, also named "Rome."

events.title: Scuttling of the Graf Spee
events.blurb: A feared commerce-raider that had sunk nine merchant ships in three months limped into a neutral harbour for repairs after a running battle with three smaller cruisers, then sat immobile while international diplomacy set a 72-hour countdown. Twenty thousand spectators lined the waterfront to watch her captain make his final decision.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1939, Montevideo. Captain Hans Langsdorff scuttled the Admiral Graf Spee at 8:55 PM rather than risk his crew in what he believed was an overwhelming British trap. Three days later he wrapped himself in the ship's battle ensign and shot himself. The trap was largely bluff.

events.title: Wannsee Conference
events.blurb: Fifteen senior government and police officials gathered for a 90-minute meeting at a lakeside villa to coordinate the administrative, transportation, and security apparatus required to murder every Jewish person across an entire continent — a project already underway in the east that now needed to be extended westward in an organised and efficient manner.
events.revealBlurb: January 20, 1942, at a villa in the Berlin suburb of Wannsee. The meeting lasted 90 minutes and was followed by lunch. The Wannsee Protocol — the only surviving copy — was found after the war hidden in a filing cabinet. Not a single one of the 15 attendees objected to what was discussed.

events.title: Battle of Anzio
events.blurb: 36,000 Allied troops landed almost unopposed on a beach 33 miles south of a major ancient capital, achieving complete surprise — then paused to consolidate rather than advancing, giving the enemy four days to rush in reinforcements and pin the beachhead into a cramped salient that became one of the bloodiest killing grounds of the Italian campaign.
events.revealBlurb: January 22 – June 4, 1944 — Operation Shingle. The initial landing met no resistance; soldiers reportedly bought wine and sat in cafes. Field Marshal Kesselring had the beachhead surrounded within a week. Allied forces took 34,000 American and 10,000 British casualties over four months before finally breaking out. Propaganda claimed "the largest self-supporting beachhead in history."

events.title: Death of Hitler
events.blurb: The dictator who had triggered the continent's most destructive conflict, directed the murder of millions, and sworn never to be taken alive shot himself in a subterranean command centre beneath a capital city now surrounded by enemy armies, having married his companion the previous day and designated a naval admiral as his successor.
events.revealBlurb: April 30, 1945 — Hitler shot himself at approximately 3:30 PM in the Führerbunker; Eva Braun took cyanide. Their bodies were carried to the garden and burned. By explicit prior order, no intact corpse was to fall into enemy hands. Soviet forces found the remains eight days after the surrender; Stalin kept the truth of their forensic identification secret for decades.

events.title: Potsdam Conference
events.blurb: The three great powers met for the last time in an occupied defeated nation's suburbs, dividing it into occupation zones, setting reparations terms, and issuing an ultimatum to a remaining Asian adversary — while one leader discreetly mentioned to another that his country had recently successfully tested a weapon of extraordinary destructive power, which the other already knew about from spies.
events.revealBlurb: July 17 – August 2, 1945. Truman told Stalin the US had "a new weapon of unusual destructive force" — Trinity had been tested the previous day. Stalin showed no reaction; his spies had briefed him months earlier. Churchill lost the British general election mid-conference and was replaced by Clement Attlee, who turned up having learned the secrets only days before.

events.title: Apple's "1984" Super Bowl Ad
events.blurb: A 60-second commercial produced by a British director for a California computer company aired during the third quarter of the Super Bowl. The ad showed a dystopian audience of grey workers watching a Big-Brother-like speaker on a vast screen; an athletic woman in running clothes smashed the screen with a hammer. The product was the Macintosh computer. Apple's board had voted to kill the ad; the CEO insisted it air. It aired once.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 1984 — directed by Ridley Scott. The ad ran nationally only that one time; it has since been shown as a promotion or film-clip thousands of times. Macintosh sales in its first 100 days exceeded expectations. The "1984" ad is still considered one of the greatest commercials ever made.

events.title: The Simpsons Premieres
events.blurb: A half-hour animated primetime sitcom about a dysfunctional yellow-skinned family in the fictional American town of Springfield premiered as a Christmas special on a fledgling US television network. The show's acerbic satire, cartoon slapstick, and unprecedented crossover appeal — with children and adults watching together — established animation as a legitimate prime-time format. It is still in production three and a half decades later, the longest-running American scripted prime-time TV series.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1989 — the Christmas special "Simpsons Roasting on an Open Fire" on the Fox network. Created by Matt Groening from shorts he had been making for The Tracey Ullman Show since 1987. The family was named after Groening's own family except Bart, an anagram of "brat."

events.title: Milli Vanilli Grammy Stripped
events.blurb: The Recording Academy revoked a Grammy award given to a German-based pop duo nine months earlier after the duo's producer, fired in a dispute, revealed publicly that the duo had not actually sung on their multi-platinum album — other studio vocalists had. The two dreadlocked frontmen had been, in effect, models who lip-synced. The scandal ended their careers; the Recording Academy has not revoked a Grammy for any reason since.
events.revealBlurb: November 19, 1990 — Milli Vanilli (Rob Pilatus and Fab Morvan) stripped of their 1989 Best New Artist Grammy. Rob Pilatus was found dead in 1998 at 32 of an accidental overdose. Fab Morvan has continued to perform. The actual vocalists included Charles Shaw, John Davis, and Brad Howell.

events.title: Spice Girls' "Wannabe"
events.blurb: A British pop group of five young women released their debut single — a bouncy three-minute track with a rap-like opening, shot on a single take in a Lisbon hotel — hit number one in 37 countries over the following months. The five — styled "Scary," "Sporty," "Baby," "Ginger," and "Posh" — would dominate late-1990s pop culture with a "Girl Power" message that was earnest, commercial, and enormously successful. They sold 100 million records globally.
events.revealBlurb: July 8, 1996 — Spice Girls: Melanie B (Scary), Melanie C (Sporty), Emma Bunton (Baby), Geri Halliwell (Ginger), Victoria Adams (Posh). The video was shot in a single day at the Hotel Palácio in Portugal. Victoria Beckham married David Beckham in 1999; she launched a fashion career later.

events.title: Titanic Premieres in the US
events.blurb: A three-hour romantic drama set aboard a doomed ocean liner's maiden voyage opened in American cinemas after a $200 million production budget — then the most expensive film ever made. It held the record as the highest-grossing film in history for twelve years and was the first to earn $1 billion and later $2 billion worldwide.

events.title: Charlemagne Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A Frankish king, in a papal basilica in the old western imperial capital for Christmas Mass, rose from prayer to be unexpectedly crowned "Emperor of the Romans" by the pope. The coronation resurrected, at least in title, a western empire that had been extinct for 324 years, and established a relationship between popes and emperors that would shape European politics for eight centuries.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 800 — Charlemagne in Rome, crowned by Pope Leo III. Charlemagne later claimed he had been surprised — but the pope probably wouldn't have dared without his consent. The Holy Roman Empire survived in one form or another until 1806.

events.title: Walk to Canossa
events.blurb: A Holy Roman Emperor, excommunicated by the pope over who had the right to appoint bishops, traveled across the Alps in the dead of winter and stood barefoot in a hair shirt in the snow outside a mountain fortress in northern Italy for three days, begging absolution. The pope eventually let him in and lifted the excommunication. The image of imperial submission to papal authority would haunt European politics for centuries.
events.revealBlurb: January 25-28, 1077 — Henry IV before Pope Gregory VII at Canossa. "To go to Canossa" became a European idiom for humiliating capitulation. Henry later recovered his throne, marched on Rome, and installed his own antipope, so the humbling was strategic rather than spiritual.

events.title: First Crusade Takes Jerusalem
events.blurb: After a month-long siege and a three-year, 3,000-kilometre march from Europe, an army of Frankish knights and footsoldiers breached the walls of a holy city in the Levant and slaughtered its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants indiscriminately over two days — perhaps 30,000 people. The first crusader state was established with a European dynasty on the throne; it would last 88 years.
events.revealBlurb: July 15, 1099 — the siege was broken when two Flemish knights scaled a siege tower onto the wall. The leaders competed to be the first to reach the Holy Sepulchre. Godfrey of Bouillon refused the crown of a city "where his savior had worn a crown of thorns" — he was titled "Defender" instead.

events.title: Hundred Years' War Begins
events.blurb: An English king, claiming the French throne through his mother on the extinction of the main French royal line, formally renounced his homage for his continental territories and declared himself the rightful king of France. The resulting dynastic war would last 116 years across five generations, introduce the longbow as a battlefield weapon, and eventually produce the nation-states of France and England.
events.revealBlurb: 1337 — Edward III vs. Philip VI. The conflict ran in spasms with long truces, and is named "Hundred Years" only in retrospect. Joan of Arc arrived in its fifth generation; gunpowder arrived in its fourth.

events.title: Black Death Reaches Europe
events.blurb: A plague arriving by trade galley at a Sicilian port spread through Mediterranean shipping lanes and overland caravans until, over the next five years, it killed an estimated 30-60 percent of Europe's population — perhaps 50 million people. Physicians had no effective response; flagellant processions and mass pogroms of Jews did little but spread the disease faster.
events.revealBlurb: October 1347 — Messina, Sicily. Caused by Yersinia pestis, spread by the fleas of black rats. Wages for surviving laborers roughly doubled; labor scarcity began eroding feudal obligations. The plague cycled back every decade or so for the next three centuries.

events.title: First Woman Prime Minister
events.blurb: The widow of an assassinated South Asian island-nation prime minister was sworn in as his successor, becoming the first woman to lead a national government anywhere in the world. She had entered politics only after her husband's murder the previous year. She would serve three separate terms over four decades, dying in office at age 84.
events.revealBlurb: July 21, 1960 — Sirimavo Bandaranaike of Ceylon (now Sri Lanka). She led a non-aligned left-of-center government; her daughter Chandrika became president 34 years later. She died on November 13, 2000, after casting her vote in a general election.

events.title: Title IX Signed
events.blurb: A U.S. president signed sweeping education legislation whose 37 words at the start of Title IX — prohibiting sex discrimination in any education program receiving federal funds — would, over the next five decades, transform American women's participation in higher education, collegiate athletics, and professional schools. Its original target had been academic admissions; its most visible effect has been women's sports.
events.revealBlurb: June 23, 1972 — Richard Nixon. High school girls' sports participation rose from 294,000 in 1972 to 3.4 million by 2019. Title IX has also been the basis for federal rules on sexual assault in higher education — a separate, contested application.

events.title: Roe v. Wade
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that the right to privacy implicit in the 14th Amendment protected a woman's decision to terminate a pregnancy, striking down most state abortion laws. The ruling established a three-trimester framework balancing state interests against individual rights. It would remain the governing precedent for 49 years, until its overturn in 2022 returned abortion regulation to the states.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 1973 — plaintiff "Jane Roe" was Norma McCorvey, who never actually had the abortion. She changed her position on the issue multiple times before her death in 2017. The ruling was overturned by Dobbs v. Jackson on June 24, 2022.

events.title: Battle of the Sexes
events.blurb: A 29-year-old women's tennis champion beat a 55-year-old former men's Wimbledon champion in straight sets at a televised exhibition match at a Houston indoor arena, before 30,000 spectators and an estimated 90 million television viewers worldwide. The older player had spent months mocking women's tennis in the press; he entered the arena on a rickshaw pulled by models in skimpy outfits and gave her a Sugar Daddy lollipop at the net.
events.revealBlurb: September 20, 1973 — Billie Jean King beat Bobby Riggs 6-4, 6-3, 6-3 at the Houston Astrodome. King had threatened to boycott the US Open unless prize money was equal; Forest Hills agreed in time for the tournament that August — the first Slam to do so.

events.title: Kamala Harris Becomes VP
events.blurb: A 56-year-old U.S. senator from California, whose mother had immigrated from India and father from Jamaica, was sworn in on the steps of the U.S. Capitol as the nation's 49th vice president, the first woman, first African-American, and first Asian-American to hold the office. She was sworn in by the first Latina Supreme Court justice, on two bibles: one from Justice Thurgood Marshall's widow and one from a close family friend.
events.revealBlurb: January 20, 2021 — sworn in by Justice Sonia Sotomayor. The inauguration, held two weeks after the January 6 Capitol attack, proceeded behind 25,000 National Guard troops. Harris later became the 2024 Democratic presidential nominee after Joe Biden withdrew.

events.title: Eruption of Vesuvius
events.blurb: A volcano on the Italian peninsula, dormant for centuries and believed extinct by the farmers whose vineyards clung to its slopes, erupted in a single day, burying two wealthy resort towns and their roughly 16,000 inhabitants under 6 metres of ash, pumice, and pyroclastic flow. The buried cities lay undiscovered for 1,700 years.
events.revealBlurb: August 24, 79 CE — Pompeii and Herculaneum, under Mount Vesuvius. Pliny the Younger watched from across the Bay of Naples and wrote the only eyewitness account. Volcanologists still classify massive plinian eruptions by his name.

events.title: Shaanxi Earthquake
events.blurb: The deadliest earthquake in recorded human history struck a densely populated region of northern China in the early morning, collapsing hillsides dotted with cave dwellings carved from soft loess soil. Roughly 830,000 people died — some 60 percent of the population of the affected counties. In some districts, everyone was killed.
events.revealBlurb: January 23, 1556 — Shaanxi Province, Ming Dynasty. The loess hillsides, prized for their insulation, became mass graves when the quake liquefied them. The toll remains a single-event record four and a half centuries later.

events.title: Krakatoa Eruption
events.blurb: An island volcano in the strait between two large Indonesian islands exploded in a series of detonations culminating in a final blast so loud it was heard 4,800 kilometres away and circled the planet four times as a pressure wave. The eruption generated tsunamis that killed 36,000 people on surrounding coasts; the resulting atmospheric dust produced red-green sunsets worldwide for years.
events.revealBlurb: August 27, 1883 — Krakatoa, Sunda Strait. The final explosion had an acoustic energy roughly equivalent to 200 megatons of TNT. The glow of the afterburn may be what Edvard Munch painted in The Scream a decade later.

events.title: Tunguska Event
events.blurb: A massive explosion in the atmosphere above a remote Siberian forest flattened some 80 million trees over an area of 2,150 square kilometres. Eyewitnesses 60 kilometres away were thrown from their chairs. Seismic stations across Europe registered the blast. The first scientific expedition did not reach the site for 19 years. No impact crater was ever found.
events.revealBlurb: June 30, 1908 — Tunguska, Russian Empire. Current consensus: a stony asteroid 50-60 metres across exploded about 8 kilometres up. If it had arrived five hours later, it would have hit St. Petersburg. The date is now International Asteroid Day.

events.title: Kobe Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 6.9 earthquake struck a major Japanese port city in the early morning, collapsing expressway sections and igniting fires that destroyed some 7,000 wooden houses. 6,434 people died. The initial government response was famously sluggish — organized yakuza crime syndicates distributed relief supplies before the army arrived.
events.revealBlurb: January 17, 1995 — Kobe. The elevated Hanshin Expressway fell sideways onto its support pillars, a widely published image of post-war Japanese infrastructure failure. The Aum Shinrikyo cult's Tokyo subway sarin attack followed two months later, making 1995 a traumatic year for Japan.

events.title: Botticelli's Primavera
events.blurb: A Florentine painter completed a large poplar panel for the bedroom of a Medici cousin, depicting nine mythological figures in a grove of orange trees — Venus at the centre, the Three Graces dancing, a gusting wind god chasing a nymph who is transformed into the flower-bearing goddess of spring. It is among the first Renaissance paintings to take mythological (not religious) subject matter on its own terms.
