events.revealBlurb: c. 1482 — Sandro Botticelli. The painting contains at least 500 identifiable plant species, some 190 different flowers. Botticelli was later nearly destroyed by Savonarola's movement and reportedly burned some of his own work in the bonfire of the vanities.

events.title: Munch's The Scream
events.blurb: A 30-year-old Norwegian painter completed the first version of a composition he had been sketching for years, showing a androgynous figure with an egg-shaped face and open mouth on a bridge above a blood-orange sky. The painter later wrote of the walk at dusk during which he had felt "a shriek passing through nature." He produced four versions across several decades; two have been stolen, and both were recovered.
events.revealBlurb: 1893 — Edvard Munch. The sky's colour may be real: it has been linked to the atmospheric effects of the Krakatoa eruption ten years earlier. The Oslo theft in 1994 happened during the opening ceremony of the Winter Olympics. The thieves left a note: "Thanks for the poor security."

events.title: Armory Show Opens
events.blurb: An exhibition at a New York National Guard armory introduced American audiences to European modernism at industrial scale — 1,300 paintings and sculptures by artists most had never heard of, including Matisse, Picasso, Duchamp, and Brancusi. Duchamp's "Nude Descending a Staircase No. 2" was ridiculed by a popular cartoonist as "explosion in a shingle factory" and drew crowds for exactly that reason. The show moved on to Chicago and Boston and is credited with changing the course of American art.
events.revealBlurb: February 17 to March 15, 1913 — the 69th Regiment Armory, Lexington Avenue, NYC. Around 90,000 people visited in New York alone. Theodore Roosevelt wrote a mostly-baffled review; a reproduction of the "Nude" was burned in effigy at the Chicago Art Institute.

events.title: Picasso's Guernica
events.blurb: A Spanish painter in his mid-fifties produced a 3.5-metre-tall monochrome canvas for the Spanish pavilion at a Paris international exposition, depicting the destruction of a Basque town by Nazi and Fascist bombers at the request of the Spanish Nationalist forces a month earlier. Screaming women, a dismembered soldier, a wounded horse, a bull, and a single lightbulb-like eye crowd the picture. The artist refused to have it displayed in his homeland until fascist rule there ended.
events.revealBlurb: Painted January-June 1937; exhibited July 12 at the Paris Exhibition. Picasso. The bombing of Guernica was on April 26, 1937. The painting toured the world for 40 years, then was installed in Madrid in 1981, six years after Franco's death.

events.title: Kahlo's The Two Fridas
events.blurb: A 32-year-old Mexican painter produced her largest painting — two life-sized self-portraits seated side-by-side on a bench, their hearts exposed and linked by an artery, against a stormy sky. The double figure depicted her divided heritage (her Mexican and European sides) and also the raw aftermath of her divorce from a fellow painter, which had become final three months earlier. She would remarry him a year later.
events.revealBlurb: 1939 — Frida Kahlo, shortly after divorcing Diego Rivera. Now in Mexico City's Museo de Arte Moderno. It was the largest canvas she ever painted, about 1.7 metres square. Kahlo's work reached superstar popularity only decades after her 1954 death.

events.title: Indian National Congress Founded
events.blurb: Seventy-two delegates — mostly English-educated Indian lawyers, journalists, and teachers, along with a few sympathetic Britons — met at a college in a western Indian port city for a three-day conference to petition the colonial government for greater Indian representation in its administration. The polite gathering would, over six decades, become the vehicle of a mass independence movement.
events.revealBlurb: December 28, 1885 — Bombay (now Mumbai). The prime mover was a retired British civil servant, Allan Octavian Hume, who believed organized political expression would prevent revolution. He was half right.

events.title: Non-Cooperation Movement Launched
events.blurb: A lawyer who had spent two decades in South Africa returned to his homeland, assumed leadership of the Congress party, and launched the first mass civil-disobedience campaign against British rule. Millions boycotted British schools, courts, and textiles; bonfires of foreign cloth burned across the country. He called it off abruptly 18 months later after a mob burned 22 policemen alive at a northern village.
events.revealBlurb: August 1, 1920 — Mohandas Gandhi. Law practices and schools emptied. The student Jawaharlal Nehru came home from Cambridge to join. The suspension after Chauri Chaura was controversial; many activists thought Gandhi had thrown away momentum.

events.title: Direct Action Day
events.blurb: The Muslim League called a general strike to demonstrate popular support for its demand for a separate Muslim-majority state. In one Bengali city, the strike degenerated into four days of intercommunal rioting in which a conservative estimate puts the dead at 4,000 and the displaced at over 100,000. The killings, and a corresponding wave in Bihar and Punjab, destroyed any remaining hope of an undivided dominion.
events.revealBlurb: August 16, 1946 — Calcutta. It is often called "the Great Calcutta Killing." Gandhi would fast in the city a year later to stop similar violence; it worked, but only locally and briefly. Partition followed in less than a year.

events.title: Gandhi Assassinated
events.blurb: A 78-year-old man, walking slowly across a Delhi lawn supported by two of his grandnieces, was shot three times in the chest at point-blank range by a Hindu nationalist who blamed him for indulging Muslims and accepting partition. He fell murmuring the name of a god. He had survived five previous attempts on his life.
events.revealBlurb: January 30, 1948 — the assassin was Nathuram Godse, a former editor of a Hindu nationalist newspaper. He was convicted and executed. Gandhi had warned his secretary that morning that his life's work would not be judged "until after I am dead and gone."

events.title: Constitution of India Adopted
events.blurb: A constituent assembly of 299 members, chaired by a Bombay-trained lawyer from a once-"untouchable" community, completed two years and eleven months of debate to enact the longest written national constitution in the world — 395 articles, 22 parts, 8 schedules — establishing a secular, socialist, democratic republic. It came into force on the anniversary of a 1930 declaration of complete independence.
events.revealBlurb: January 26, 1950 — B.R. Ambedkar, chair of the drafting committee. The date — Republic Day — was chosen because it marked the 20th anniversary of Congress's Purna Swaraj declaration. The final handwritten copy is illuminated by the artist Nandalal Bose.

events.title: Macintosh Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company launched a new desktop computer during a Super Bowl advertising spot, and formally introduced it at a shareholders meeting two days later. The machine had a 9-inch black-and-white screen, a mouse, a graphical user interface with icons and windows, and pull-down menus — none of which had previously shipped on a mass-market computer. It cost $2,495 and would struggle commercially against the cheaper IBM PC for years.
events.revealBlurb: January 24, 1984 — Apple Macintosh. Ridley Scott's "1984" Super Bowl ad ran on January 22. The original Mac shipped with 128KB of memory; Bill Gates had quietly promised Steve Jobs a version of MS Word for it.

events.title: Google Founded
events.blurb: Two Stanford doctoral students incorporated a search engine company whose name derived from the mathematical term for 10 to the power of 100. Their PageRank algorithm ranked results by treating hyperlinks as votes, producing more relevant results than the keyword-frequency systems that dominated at the time.

events.title: iMac Released
events.blurb: A California computer company, newly returned to profitability under a recently returned co-founder, released an all-in-one desktop machine housed in a translucent Bondi-blue plastic case, with no floppy drive, a built-in USB port, and a round puck of a mouse. Industrial designer Jonathan Ive had led the design. The machine was derided on spec by some industry press; it sold over 800,000 units in the first five months and rescued the company's consumer business.
events.revealBlurb: August 15, 1998 — Apple iMac G3, designed by Jonathan Ive under Steve Jobs. The "i" prefix, coined by copywriter Ken Segall, would carry over to iPod, iPhone, iPad, iCloud. The translucent plastic shell was revolutionary for its time.

events.title: BlackBerry Released
events.blurb: A Canadian wireless technology company released a two-way pager with a small keyboard and a monochrome screen that could also receive email. Corporate IT departments loved it — executives could finally stay in touch while traveling — and within a few years the device had become a status symbol and, later, an addiction. Users typed with thumbs on the tiny QWERTY keys; the resulting repetitive-strain injury acquired the nickname "BlackBerry thumb."
events.revealBlurb: January 19, 1999 — Research In Motion's BlackBerry 850. Chosen name because the keyboard's buttons resembled the drupelets of a blackberry fruit. The iPhone's 2007 arrival began BlackBerry's long decline; RIM pivoted to BlackBerry Ltd. and left hardware in 2016.

events.title: First Android Phone Released
events.blurb: A Taiwanese handset maker released the first commercial phone running an open-source mobile operating system developed by a Silicon Valley search-engine company, available through a US mobile carrier. The device had a physical keyboard that slid out from under the screen; unlike the rival iPhone, users could install apps from anywhere, replace the default apps, and generally modify the device at will. Open-ecosystem Android would grow to dominate global smartphone market share.
events.revealBlurb: October 22, 2008 — T-Mobile G1 (HTC Dream), running Android 1.0. Google had quietly acquired Android Inc. for $50 million in 2005. By 2013 more than half of smartphones sold ran Android; today it's over 70 percent globally.

events.title: NAACP Founded
events.blurb: A biracial group of activists, scholars, and newspaper editors met at a New York conference on the centennial of Abraham Lincoln's birth to establish an organization dedicated to fighting racial discrimination through legal action and public advocacy. W.E.B. Du Bois, the Harvard-trained sociologist, edited its magazine The Crisis; its lawyers would eventually argue Brown v. Board of Education.
events.revealBlurb: February 12, 1909 — National Association for the Advancement of Colored People. It was founded partly in response to the Springfield, Illinois race riot the year before. Du Bois served as editor of The Crisis for 24 years.

events.title: Emmett Till Murdered
events.blurb: A 14-year-old Black boy visiting family in a rural Southern state was abducted from his great-uncle's home in the middle of the night, tortured, shot, and thrown into a river with a cotton-gin fan tied around his neck. His mother insisted on an open-casket funeral so the world could see what had been done to her son. Photographs of the mutilated body, published in Jet magazine, galvanized a generation.
events.revealBlurb: August 28, 1955 — Money, Mississippi. His accuser, Carolyn Bryant, admitted decades later she had lied about the encounter. Her husband and his half-brother were acquitted by an all-white jury, then sold their confession to Look magazine knowing they couldn't be retried.

events.title: Greensboro Sit-Ins
events.blurb: Four Black college freshmen sat down at the segregated lunch counter of a downtown variety store in a North Carolina city and politely ordered coffee. When refused service, they stayed seated until closing. They returned the next day with more students. Within two months, similar sit-ins had spread to 55 cities in 13 states, and the variety-store chain desegregated its counters.
events.revealBlurb: February 1, 1960 — Woolworth's lunch counter, Greensboro. The original four were students at North Carolina A&T State University: Ezell Blair, Franklin McCain, Joseph McNeil, David Richmond. Part of the counter is now in the Smithsonian.

events.title: Martin Luther King Jr. Assassinated
events.blurb: Stepping onto the balcony outside Room 306 of a Tennessee motel where he was staying while supporting a sanitation workers' strike, the country's most prominent civil rights leader was shot once with a high-powered rifle from across the street. He died an hour later at a nearby hospital. He was 39. Riots broke out in more than 100 American cities within hours of the news.
events.revealBlurb: April 4, 1968 — Lorraine Motel, Memphis. His killer, escaped convict James Earl Ray, was captured in London two months later. The night before, King had ended a speech with: "I've been to the mountaintop. I may not get there with you, but we, as a people, will get to the Promised Land."

events.title: Shirley Chisholm's Presidential Run
events.blurb: A Brooklyn congresswoman, four years after becoming the first Black woman elected to the U.S. Congress, announced her candidacy for the presidency. She was the first African-American to seek a major party's nomination and the first woman to seek the Democratic one. Her slogan was "Unbought and Unbossed." She earned 152 convention delegates before Senator George McGovern won the nomination.
events.revealBlurb: January 25, 1972. She had to sue to be included in televised debates. She survived three assassination attempts during the campaign. "When I ran," she said later, "I ran because someone had to do it first."

events.title: FIFA Founded
events.blurb: Representatives of seven European national football associations — Belgium, Denmark, France, Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland — met at a Paris sports association's offices and established an international governing body for the sport. England, which had invented the modern codified game and considered itself the natural authority, declined to attend, joined in 1905, and withdrew multiple times over subsequent decades in petty disputes. The organization would run the World Cup from 1930 on.
events.revealBlurb: May 21, 1904 — Fédération Internationale de Football Association, Paris. Its first president was Robert Guérin. FIFA now has 211 member associations, more than the UN. Its headquarters moved to Zurich in 1932 and have been there since.

events.title: First Super Bowl
events.blurb: The championship game between the established National Football League and the upstart American Football League — which had been playing for seven seasons and had just agreed to merge — was held at a Los Angeles stadium. 61,946 fans attended, leaving 30,000 seats empty; tickets had cost $12. The NFL's Green Bay Packers beat the AFL's Kansas City Chiefs 35-10. Both CBS and NBC televised the game, with separate commentators and camera crews, because the networks could not agree who would get exclusive rights.
events.revealBlurb: January 15, 1967 — the AFL-NFL World Championship Game (renamed "Super Bowl" in year III). Chiefs owner Lamar Hunt had proposed the name jokingly, inspired by his daughter's Super Ball toy. The Super Bowl is now the single most-watched annual TV event in the US.

events.title: Black Power Salute in Mexico
events.blurb: Two African-American sprinters, having just won gold and bronze in the 200 metres at a Summer Olympics, stepped onto the medal podium shoeless, wearing black socks, and raised black-gloved fists as the U.S. national anthem played. The Australian silver medallist on the second step wore an Olympic Project for Human Rights badge in solidarity. The gesture — a deliberate human rights protest — cost the two Americans their Olympic careers; they were suspended from the U.S. team and booed on their return home.
events.revealBlurb: October 16, 1968 — Tommie Smith and John Carlos; the Australian was Peter Norman. Norman was subsequently ostracized by the Australian team; the two Americans bore his pall at his 2006 funeral. A 7-metre statue of the podium moment stands today on the San Jose State University campus.

events.title: Brady's Super Bowl LI Comeback
events.blurb: A New England Patriots team down 28-3 to the Atlanta Falcons in the third quarter of a Super Bowl came back to tie, forcing the first overtime in Super Bowl history, and won on a two-yard touchdown run that completed the largest comeback in title-game history. The team's 39-year-old quarterback won his record fifth Super Bowl championship and was named MVP for the fourth time. He would win two more Super Bowls over the following five years.
events.revealBlurb: February 5, 2017 — Super Bowl LI, Patriots 34, Falcons 28 OT, at NRG Stadium, Houston. Tom Brady. The Falcons had to stop themselves from ordering Super Bowl champion merchandise at halftime. Brady was the oldest Super Bowl MVP in history (at the time).

events.title: Kobe Bryant Dies
events.blurb: A 41-year-old retired basketball star, his 13-year-old daughter, and seven other passengers died when their private helicopter crashed into a hillside in thick fog outside Los Angeles while en route to a youth basketball game. The retired player had won five NBA championships, two Olympic golds, and the nickname "Black Mamba" during a 20-year career entirely with the Los Angeles Lakers. The crash prompted an outpouring of mourning around the world.
events.revealBlurb: January 26, 2020 — Kobe and Gianna Bryant. National Transportation Safety Board findings attributed the crash to pilot error in poor visibility. His 2017 jersey-retirement ceremony at Staples Center saw both his numbers (8 and 24) raised to the rafters — the only player in franchise history with multiple retired numbers.

events.title: Lend-Lease Act Signed
events.blurb: A nation officially at peace passed legislation allowing its president to lend, lease, or otherwise transfer war materials to any country whose defence he deemed vital to national security, bypassing a strict neutrality law without technically entering the conflict. The first shipments moved within weeks, directed at an island nation running critically short of everything.
events.revealBlurb: March 11, 1941 — FDR signed H.R. 1776 (the bill number was a deliberate wink). By the end of the programme, the US had shipped $50 billion in supplies — equivalent to roughly $800 billion today — to 38 countries. The Soviet Union received about 17 million tons of equipment, including 400,000 jeeps and trucks.

events.title: Dieppe Raid
events.blurb: Roughly 6,000 troops — mostly Canadians — landed in daylight on a heavily defended beach overlooked by cliffs and were cut down before many could clear the waterline, suffering nearly 60 percent casualties in under ten hours. Planners later claimed the catastrophic failure provided lessons that saved countless lives in subsequent amphibious operations.
events.revealBlurb: August 19, 1942 — Operation Jubilee. Of 4,963 Canadians who embarked, only 2,210 returned to England; 907 were killed and 1,946 taken prisoner. The Germans, who had received advance intelligence, held their positions with minimal effort. Churchill admitted privately it was "a very heavy and grievous loss."

events.title: Battle of Stalingrad
events.blurb: For six months, a city named after a living leader was fought over house by house, factory floor by factory floor, in temperatures reaching minus 40 degrees, as an encircled attacking force slowly starved and froze while its commander received a field marshal's baton and an order never to surrender. The first capitulation of an entire German field army in the war followed 12 days later.
events.revealBlurb: August 1942 – February 2, 1943. Of the 330,000 who entered the Stalingrad pocket, 91,000 surrendered — including 24 generals and Field Marshal Friedrich Paulus. Fewer than 6,000 of those prisoners ever returned to Germany. Hitler promoted Paulus to Field Marshal the day before surrender, noting no German field marshal had ever been taken alive.

events.title: Battle of Leyte Gulf
events.blurb: Over four days, 282 warships clashed in four separate engagements across several hundred thousand square kilometres of open ocean — the largest naval battle in history by tonnage and personnel — as one navy committed virtually everything it had left to stop an invasion and the other deployed over 300 ships to press it through.
events.revealBlurb: October 23–26, 1944. Japan used its remaining fleet carriers as decoys with almost no aircraft aboard. A small force of US destroyers and escort carriers somehow bluffed a vastly superior Japanese battleship force into retreating at the Battle of Samar — one of the most improbable tactical reversals of the war. Japan also deployed kamikaze suicide aircraft in force for the first time.

events.title: Liberation of Auschwitz
events.blurb: Soviet soldiers opened the gates of a vast camp complex to find several thousand survivors too ill to have been force-marched away, alongside 1.2 million items of women's clothing, 43,000 pairs of shoes, seven tonnes of human hair, and industrial quantities of Zyklon B — physical evidence of the systematic murder of more than a million people.
events.revealBlurb: January 27, 1945. The 60th Army of the 1st Ukrainian Front liberated roughly 7,000 remaining prisoners. The SS had dynamited the crematoria weeks earlier to destroy evidence. January 27 is now the United Nations' International Holocaust Remembrance Day. The surviving Sonderkommando testimonies buried in the ash confirmed what the physical evidence already showed.

events.title: Rubik's Cube Global Craze
events.blurb: A 3×3 mechanical puzzle cube invented six years earlier by a Hungarian architecture professor became a global bestseller after licensed international distribution began. Over 100 million units sold in the first three years. Books of solutions appeared on bestseller lists. The puzzle's simplicity — six colours, 43 quintillion possible states, a single solved configuration — caught people who had never bought a toy in their lives. World championships began in 1982.
events.revealBlurb: 1981 — Ernő Rubik had patented the cube in 1975; it went international in 1980. The first world championship was in Budapest, June 5, 1982; the current world record for solving it is under 3.05 seconds (Max Park, June 2023). The cube remains in continuous production.

events.title: Tylenol Murders
events.blurb: Seven people in the Chicago area died after taking over-the-counter acetaminophen capsules that had been laced with potassium cyanide by an unknown tamperer. The crisis triggered a nationwide recall of 31 million bottles, launched the tamper-resistant packaging industry, and reshaped pharmaceutical manufacturing standards permanently. Johnson & Johnson's swift and transparent response became a classic case study in crisis management. The killer was never identified.
events.revealBlurb: September 29-October 1, 1982 — seven deaths in Chicago suburbs. Pills had been purchased, tampered with, and returned to drugstore shelves. James William Lewis, a former suspect, died in 2023 maintaining his innocence. Tamper-proof packaging became a federal mandate within six months.

events.title: We Are the World Recorded
events.blurb: Forty-five American pop stars gathered at a Los Angeles recording studio after the annual American Music Awards ceremony to record a charity single for African famine relief, written by two headliners in a single evening. The recording session ran until 8 AM. The single sold over 20 million copies and raised more than $63 million. Its producer had hung a sign at the studio entrance reading: "Check your ego at the door."
events.revealBlurb: January 28, 1985 — written by Michael Jackson and Lionel Richie; produced by Quincy Jones. Participating artists included Stevie Wonder, Bruce Springsteen, Bob Dylan, Diana Ross, and Ray Charles. The sign was Jones's idea. A 2024 Netflix documentary rehashed the making of the track.

events.title: Challenger Disintegration
events.blurb: Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch when a rubber O-ring seal on the right solid rocket booster failed in overnight temperatures that had dropped to -8 °C, allowing combustion gases to breach the joint and sever the external tank. All seven crew members were killed, including Christa McAuliffe, who had been selected from more than 11,000 applicants for NASA's Teacher in Space program.
events.revealBlurb: January 28, 1986 — STS-51-L. Engineers at Morton Thiokol had urged a launch delay the night before, citing O-ring behavior in cold temperatures; NASA managers overruled them. The crew cabin survived the initial breakup intact and fell for nearly three minutes before striking the Atlantic at roughly 320 km/h.

events.title: Kurt Cobain Dies
events.blurb: A 27-year-old grunge-rock frontman was found dead of a self-inflicted shotgun wound in the greenhouse above the garage of his Seattle home. He had struggled with heroin addiction, a collapsed marriage, chronic stomach pain, and the deep anxieties of sudden fame. His suicide note quoted a line from a Neil Young song: "It's better to burn out than to fade away." A public memorial at Seattle Center drew 7,000 mourners.
events.revealBlurb: April 5, 1994 — Kurt Cobain of Nirvana. The body was not discovered for three days, by an electrician installing a security system. Conspiracy theories have persisted for decades. Cobain joined the "27 Club" of pop musicians who died at that age, including Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, Jim Morrison, and Amy Winehouse.

events.title: Explorer 1 — First US Satellite
events.blurb: A Juno I rocket launched the United States' first satellite from Cape Canaveral, placing an 8.3 kg cylinder into an elliptical orbit that reached 2,550 km altitude. The satellite's Geiger–Müller tube detected a region of intense radiation surrounding Earth — data that led James Van Allen to identify the radiation belts bearing his name.
events.revealBlurb: January 31, 1958 — Explorer 1. The US had been beaten to orbit by Sputnik 1 and Sputnik 2 in the previous three months. In a press conference photo, three scientists hoisted a full-scale model over their heads in triumph — the actual satellite weighed less than a toaster oven. Explorer 1 remained in orbit for 12 years.

events.title: Voyager 1 Launch
events.blurb: NASA launched Voyager 1 on a trajectory exploiting a once-in-176-year alignment of the outer planets, allowing a single spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn using gravitational slingshots. The probe carries a gold-plated copper phonograph record containing sounds, music, and images representing life on Earth, selected by a committee chaired by Carl Sagan.
events.revealBlurb: September 5, 1977 — Voyager 1. It launched 16 days after its twin, Voyager 2, yet arrived at Jupiter first due to a faster trajectory. In 2012 it became the first human-made object to enter interstellar space. As of 2024 it is more than 24 billion km from Earth — so far that its radio signals, traveling at light speed, take over 22 hours to arrive.

events.title: Hubble Space Telescope Launch
events.blurb: Space Shuttle Discovery deployed the Hubble Space Telescope into a 612 km orbit, positioning a 2.4-meter primary mirror above Earth's atmosphere to capture ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light without atmospheric distortion. The primary mirror was later found to have been ground 2.2 micrometers too flat — a spherical aberration correctable only by a servicing mission.
events.revealBlurb: April 24, 1990 — STS-31. The mirror flaw came from a testing lens installed backward by 1.3 mm. Three years later, astronauts installed corrective optics during the first Hubble servicing mission — essentially fitting the telescope with contact lenses. Hubble has since produced more than 1.5 million observations.

events.title: Mir Space Station Deorbit
events.blurb: Russia deliberately deorbited the Mir space station after 15 years of continuous operation, using three burns from a docked Progress cargo spacecraft to lower its orbit until it reentered the atmosphere over the South Pacific. Most of the station burned up during reentry, but approximately 1,500 kg of debris survived and splashed into the ocean between Australia and Chile.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 2001 — Mir deorbit. Mir had been in orbit so long that cosmonauts reported the walls were alive with mold. A Russian company sold pay-per-view rights to watch the reentry from a chartered aircraft. Japan offered to purchase and keep the station operational; the deal fell through over cost. It had been visited by 104 cosmonauts and astronauts from 12 nations.

events.title: Columbia Reentry Breakup
events.blurb: Space Shuttle Columbia disintegrated over Texas and Louisiana during reentry, killing all seven crew members 16 minutes before its scheduled landing. A 1.2 kg piece of insulating foam had struck the leading edge of the left wing at liftoff 16 days earlier, breaching a reinforced carbon-carbon thermal protection panel and allowing superheated plasma to enter the wing structure during descent.
events.revealBlurb: February 1, 2003 — STS-107. Columbia was the oldest shuttle in the fleet, on its 28th mission. Debris was recovered across 2,000 km of Texas and Louisiana; some experiments in sealed canisters survived, including a container of worms (C. elegans) that lived through the breakup. It was the second shuttle lost in 113 flights.

events.title: Don Giovanni Premieres
events.blurb: A 31-year-old composer conducted the premiere of his two-act opera about a dissolute nobleman's pursuit of women and eventual descent into Hell, before Prague nobility at the Estates Theatre. According to his librettist, the overture was composed the night before the premiere while the composer's wife kept him awake through the small hours with punch and fairy tales.

events.title: First Jazz Recording
events.blurb: Five white musicians from New Orleans, working under the slightly misspelled name "Original Dixieland Jass Band," recorded two sides for a Victor label at a New York studio: "Livery Stable Blues" and "Dixie Jass Band One Step." The 78 sold a million copies, breaking sales records, and introduced the word "jazz" to most Americans. Black New Orleans musicians had been playing the style for years; the first commercial recording went to imitators.
events.revealBlurb: February 26, 1917 — recorded in NYC; released March 7, 1917. The ODJB's cornetist Nick LaRocca later claimed, implausibly, to have invented jazz. The ethical irony of white performers first commercializing a Black art form was noted at the time and has only grown.

events.title: Elvis Records "That's All Right"
events.blurb: During a break in a fruitless recording session in Memphis, a 19-year-old truck driver began playing an uptempo blues song with such energy that the studio owner halted the session, rewound the tape, and asked him to do it again from the start. The recording blended country and rhythm-and-blues in a style that had no existing commercial category.

events.title: Kind of Blue Released
events.blurb: A 33-year-old trumpet player released a five-track album recorded in two half-day sessions in a converted Manhattan church. He had given the musicians — including a young tenor saxophonist he had just hired — only short modal sketches, not written music, and one of the tracks was a single take. The album would become the best-selling jazz record of all time, its influence extending to rock, classical minimalism, and film scoring.
events.revealBlurb: August 17, 1959 — Miles Davis at 30th Street Studio, NYC. Sidemen: John Coltrane, Cannonball Adderley, Bill Evans, Paul Chambers, Jimmy Cobb. It has sold over 5 million copies in the US alone, received quintuple-platinum status.

events.title: Beatles' Final Public Performance
events.blurb: A four-piece rock band performed without announcement on the roof of their recording company's London headquarters for 42 minutes in near-freezing winter temperatures, drawing a crowd of hundreds in the street below before police ended the show citing noise complaints. The impromptu rooftop set was their last performance together in front of a live audience.

events.title: Pong Released in Arcades
events.blurb: A black-and-white rectangle containing two paddles and a bouncing dot was installed in a Sunnyvale, California tavern as a hardware test. The test machine broke within days — not from malfunction, but because the coin slot had overflowed with quarters. Atari scrambled to ship units nationwide, and the commercial video game industry was born.
events.revealBlurb: November 29, 1972 — Atari Inc., founded that June by Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney, shipped Pong to arcades. The Andy Capp's Tavern prototype jammed after a week because it held too many coins.

events.title: Pokémon Red and Green Released in Japan
events.blurb: A game about capturing and training pocket monsters on a handheld with a dying link cable had been in development for six years and nearly bankrupted its studio twice. It released quietly on a console most retailers considered obsolete. Within months it had detonated into the fastest-growing entertainment franchise in Japanese history.
events.revealBlurb: February 27, 1996 — Pokémon Red and Green launched for Game Boy in Japan. By the end of 1996 they had sold 3.6 million copies in Japan alone; the franchise has since generated over $150 billion, making it the highest-grossing media franchise in history.

events.title: Final Fantasy VII Released in Japan
events.blurb: A Japanese role-playing game with pre-rendered 3D backgrounds, full orchestral-style music, and a story involving ecological collapse and corporate villainy sold out PlayStation consoles across Japan before it even launched. On release day it sold 1.75 million copies in a single country in a single day.
events.revealBlurb: January 31, 1997 — Final Fantasy VII launched in Japan for PlayStation. It sold 2.3 million copies in its first three days and over 6 million by 1998. Its western release September 7, 1997, introduced the JRPG genre to millions. The 2020 remake sold over 7 million copies in under four days.

events.title: The Sims Released
events.blurb: A game in which you build a house and manage the life of a simulated person — feeding them, making them use the bathroom, watching them catch fire if left unattended too long — became the best-selling PC game of the year, and then 2001, and then the best-selling PC game of all time. More than half its players were women, permanently disproving every assumption the games industry held about its audience.
events.revealBlurb: February 4, 2000 — Maxis and EA released The Sims for Windows. It sold 1.77 million copies in North America in its first year. The Sims overtook Myst to become the best-selling PC game ever in 2002. The franchise has sold over 70 million copies.

events.title: Pokémon GO Launches
events.blurb: A mobile game using GPS and augmented reality sent tens of millions of people into parks, cemeteries, and government buildings to catch fictional creatures on their phones. It broke multiple App Store records in its first 24 hours. Police stations issued public statements asking players not to enter. Central Park held impromptu gatherings of thousands at midnight.
events.revealBlurb: July 6, 2016 — Pokémon GO launched in the United States, Australia, and New Zealand. It surpassed 100 million downloads in under 30 days and generated $207 million in its first month — the highest ever for a mobile game. Lifetime revenue has surpassed $6 billion.
